chunks: Ali ibn Mahziyar from Fadala from Abdullah ibn Sinan said:

My father asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the one who lends his garment to someone he knows eats garlic and drinks wine, and then takes it back; does he pray in it before washing it? He said, 'He does not pray in it until he washes it.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is to be understood as indicating preference (istihbab) because the default state of all things is purity, and washing a garment is not obligatory except after knowing that it contains impurity, and this narrator has narrated the opposite of this report.

key_terms.يُعِيرُ: to lend or give on loan

ai.seo_question: Do I need to wash my clothes if I lend them to someone who eats garlic or drinks wine?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration where the Imam advises washing garments lent to those known to consume impurities like garlic or wine before prayer. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan provides crucial scholarly context, interpreting the ruling as *mustahabb* (recommended) rather than obligatory, grounded in the principle that the default state of all things is purity (*asl al-taharah*) unless specific impurity is confirmed. This highlights the Shia juristic balance between caution in ritual purity and avoiding undue hardship in daily transactions.
